posts.title: GRAMMY AWARD-WINNING PRODUCER EASY MO BEE TO LAUNCH ICONIC BEATS WITH LIVE DJ SET AND BOOK SIGNING AT TRENTON BOOK FAIR
posts.author: Matias Regis, Jr.
posts.summary:
WCIP brings its Street Lit House Party experience to Trenton on October 10, featuring Easy Mo
Bee and a live house music set by DJ Jonathan Lewis, co-author of House Music 101.
posts.content:
TRENTON, NJ — Grammy Award-winning producer Easy Mo Bee will bring ICONIC BEATS:
Easy Mo Bee’s Unforgettable Tracks for Biggie, Tupac, & Hip-Hop’s Greatest to life at the
Trenton Book Fair and Block Party on October 10, marking his first public book signing for the
new memoir and an opportunity for audiences to experience the music behind his story.
Rather than simply signing books, Easy Mo Bee will take the turntables for an approximately
one-hour DJ set featuring music connected to his career and the stories explored in ICONIC
BEATS. The appearance is part of WCIP’s Street Lit House Party experience, which brings
books, music and live cultural programming together.

EASY MO BEE BRINGS THE STORIES BEHIND THE MUSIC TO THE STAGE


In ICONIC BEATS, Easy Mo Bee opens up in his own voice about the music, moments and
principles behind some of hip-hop’s most unforgettable records. The book takes readers inside
the making of records, the art of sampling, the politics of credit and the culture that shaped his
career, including his work connected to Biggie, Tupac, Miles Davis, Busta Rhymes, Craig Mack,
Alicia Keys and others.

The book features a foreword by hip-hop legend Big Daddy Kane and includes a special chapter
focused on Easy Mo Bee’s work with Miles Davis on Doo-Bop. Together, those elements give
readers a closer look at both the career and creative process behind the records.

“We’re not bringing Easy Mo Bee to Trenton just to sit behind a table and sign books. We’re
bringing the stories and the music together. He’ll sign ICONIC BEATS and get behind the
turntables to play the records connected to his journey. Then DJ Jonathan Lewis will take us into
the world of house music. That’s what Street Lit House Party is about: bringing the culture in the
books to life.” says Wahida Clark, Founder, Wahida Clark Innovative Publishing

FROM HIP-HOP TO HOUSE MUSIC

The Trenton experience will also feature DJ Jonathan Lewis, co-author of House Music 101,
with a one-hour house music set.

Lewis’s appearance expands the Street Lit House Party experience beyond a single author or
genre, connecting the history documented in the books with the music and culture that continue
to shape audiences today.

The program will also spotlight WCIP titles and authors, including House Music 101, Muqarabun
and Rent Money, giving attendees an opportunity to discover new stories alongside the live
music experience.

Trenton Book Fair and Block Party
October 10, 2026
Trenton, New Jersey
Featured experience:

● Easy Mo Bee’s first ICONIC BEATS book signing
● Approximately one-hour Easy Mo Bee DJ set
● DJ Jonathan Lewis one-hour house music set
● House Music 101 and participating authors
● WCIP titles including Muqarabun and Rent Money
● Street Lit House Party programming

Media interested in covering the October 10 appearance may request interview and event
coverage information through WCIP. Any advance interview opportunities involving Easy Mo
Bee will be coordinated in accordance with the campaign’s existing media commitments.

ABOUT WAHIDA CLARK INNOVATIVE PUBLISHING

Wahida Clark Innovative Publishing (WCIP) is an independent publishing company founded by
award-winning author Wahida Clark. WCIP publishes compelling, culturally relevant books and
develops opportunities that connect authors and their stories with readers and audiences
through innovative publishing, marketing, media and promotional initiatives. WCIP is committed
to amplifying distinctive voices and bringing powerful stories to wider audiences across literary
and cultural communities.

posts.title: Jefferson Township Kiwanis Club Named Number One New Club in the Nation
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: New Jersey District Kiwanis International Governor Frank Cahill presents Yvonne Ioffredo, Treasurer of the Kiwanis Club of Jefferson Township, with a plaque recognizing the club as the number one new Kiwanis club in the nation.
posts.content:
JEFFERSON TOWNSHIP -- New Jersey District Kiwanis International Governor Frank Cahill presents Yvonne Ioffredo, Treasurer of the Kiwanis Club of Jefferson Township, with a plaque congratulating the club on achieving the highest number of member registrations at its organizational meeting in January.

Of all the clubs chartered during the service year, the Kiwanis Club of Jefferson Township ranked number one in the entire United States. Cahill's theme for his year was "Double Down with Frank," and Jefferson far exceeded the membership required to charter a new Kiwanis club. The presentation was made during the New Jersey District Kiwanis Convention, held September 17–20 at the Tropicana in Atlantic City.

Kiwanis International's mission is to empower communities to improve the world by making lasting differences in the lives of children.

For information, email fcahill@njkiwanis.org or call (973) 559-6000.

posts.title: NECANN New Jersey 2026 Recap: Inside the Atlantic City Cannabis Convention
posts.author: Bridget Papino
posts.summary: Go inside NECANN New Jersey 2026 in Atlantic City with We Are Jersey and Beast Media, including two days of panels, brands, interviews and the NECANN Cup.
posts.content:
By We Are Jersey | On-site interviews by Adrianna Bauldock | Media partners with Beast Media

Atlantic City put New Jersey Cannabis in One Room

For two packed days, the Atlantic City Convention Center became a meeting ground for the people shaping cannabis in the Garden State. NECANN New Jersey 2026 brought operators, dispensary teams, cultivators, manufacturers, educators, advocates, investors, service providers, creators and curious attendees together on September 18 and 19 for a convention that moved easily between serious business and genuine community.

We Are Jersey attended as a media partner alongside Beast Media, with Adrianna Bauldock on the floor interviewing guests, speakers, brands and vendors throughout the weekend. The result was more than a trade-show walk-through. It was a close-up look at an industry asking bigger questions: Who gets to participate? What does sustainable growth look like? How do companies earn trust? And how can New Jersey build an ecosystem that reflects the communities that carried cannabis culture long before legalization?

The short answer: through education, collaboration and visibility. From policy discussions and operational strategy to women-led networking, academic research, brand building, wellness and the NECANN Cup, this year's program made room for nearly every part of the conversation.

What Made NECANN New Jersey 2026 Worth The Trip

NECANN describes its New Jersey convention as a business-to-business event focused entirely on the state's cannabis market. That focus could be felt across the floor. Exhibitors were not simply handing out promotional items; many were explaining products, comparing services, discussing regulations and building relationships that could turn into real business after the badges came off.

The convention ran from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Friday and 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Saturday at the Atlantic City Convention Center. The main exhibit hall held brand booths, vendor activations and open-access programming, while additional sessions took place in Rooms 318 and 319. The Beast Media Stage sat at the intersection of business, leadership, policy and culture, giving the show a strong New Jersey voice. A dedicated Blunt Brunch women's lounge added its own community-centered programming, and Saturday also included a free cannabis-conviction expungement clinic presented by Blaze Responsibly.

Outside the formal sessions, NECANN created multiple ways to keep conversations moving: a Thursday pre-show reception for eligible badge holders, Friday's day-one mixer at the Treehouse, the official after-party at Tennessee Avenue Beer Hall, and a free shuttle connecting the convention with High Rollers Dispensary. Those details mattered because some of the weekend's most valuable moments happened between panels, in booth aisles and during the follow-up conversation after an introduction.

Day One Combined Policy, Science, Leadership and Practical Growth

Friday opened with a schedule that showed how wide the cannabis industry has become. On the Beast Media Stage, From Cannabis to Campus: Building the Next Industry Pipeline connected cannabis and psychedelics research with higher education and workforce development through Tauhid Chappell, Bria-Necole Diggs, Dr. Ara Karakashian and Dr. Denise Vidot. The inaugural symposium kickoff extended that academic lens through a large group of researchers, educators and students, including Anthony Alfonso, Nyomi Barrick-Wommack, Mavis Berko, Ciné Brown, Jasmine Davis, Sunehera Hasib, Kayla Hearon, Benedictus Hlormenu, Rob Mejia, Tomiwa Oyedokun, Hayley Palmer and others from institutions including the University of Miami, Rutgers University and Stockton University.

The stage then shifted toward questions that are especially relevant in New Jersey. Joseph Artim, Adam Goldner, Sam Reichbart and Michael Wiehl addressed home cultivation and access during The Garden State Without a Garden. Danielle A. Drummond, Gretchen Gailey, Kate Miller and Kathleen Olivastro centered women advancing into executive leadership. Regional officials Ava Concepcion, John Kagia and Joshua Sanderlin discussed what federal rescheduling could mean across Northeast state lines.

In the seminar rooms, attendees could dig into the effect of federal rescheduling on New Jersey cannabis businesses, practical chemistry for producers and retailers, the path from licensure to successful operations, AI efficiency for cannabis retailers, economic inclusion after prohibition, patient-centered business strategy, marketing beyond the existing cannabis audience, and the realities of scaling vape production. Together, those sessions reflected the full pressure of operating in a young regulated market: compliance, education, margins, production, customer acquisition and long-term credibility all have to work at the same time.

The Blunt Brunch space gave Friday a more intimate rhythm. Coffee and pastries led into Leading Out Loud, a conversation about visibility, influence, confidence and personal branding. Speed networking gave attendees a structured way to move beyond small talk, and the program closed with community connections and a women-in-cannabis group photo.

Friday Programming at a Glance

Blunt Brunch Coffee, Pastries and Community Welcome

Practical Chemistry for Producers and Retailers — Jeff Rawson

Inaugural Symposium Kickoff — Anthony Alfonso, Nyomi Barrick-Wommack, Mavis Berko, Ciné Brown, Jasmine Davis, Bria-Necole Diggs, Sunehera Hasib, Kayla Hearon, Benedictus Hlormenu, Kieran Kenig, Rob Mejia, Mark Moffatt, Josue Munguia, Tomiwa Oyedokun, Hayley Palmer, Jessica Phillips and Bright Tamakloe

The Garden State Without a Garden — Joseph Artim, Adam Goldner, Sam Reichbart and Michael Wiehl

The Path to Licensure and Operating: The Power of Collaborative Relationships — Will Bowden

Leading Out Loud: Building Visibility, Influence and Confidence in Business — JM Balbuena, Jennifer Makris and Katie Motta

AI Efficiency for Cannabis Retailers — Marcus Johnson-Smith

Speed Networking

From Raw Flower to Retail Ready: Scaling Vape Production in Practice — Bernard Gruberg, Tim Marsh, Gustavo Reyes Jr. and Isaiah Winn

Community Connections, Group Photo and Closing Celebration

Day Two Brought Culture, Consumer Experience And The Future Into Focus

Saturday began with Cafe con Comunidad, a Hispanic Heritage Month gathering presented through Blunt Brunch and the Latino Cannabis Alliance. The morning conversation honored immigrant stories, leadership and connection before the larger schedule accelerated across the hall.

Programming examined how cannabis spaces can become more trust-based and healing through Jennifer DeWalt, how cultivators can protect profitability against high energy costs through Dominic Galanti, Jim Kordoban and Mikhail Sagal, and how Queenee Gonzalez, Sativa Papi, Audris B. Torres and Toast Vargas are using personal branding and digital media to build influence. Built for the Block brought John Brody, Dharsh Casinathen, Joshua Krane and Tenisha Victor together to ask what authentic New Jersey cannabis branding looks like when a company is building with the state rather than simply selling into it.

One of the day's most visible conversations, Drink the Plant, explored cannabis beverages through health, wellness, public policy and product innovation with Leo Bridgewater, Matthew Lovett, Wesley McWhite and Reggie ‘Redman’ Noble. On the Beast Media Stage, Brandi Hester-Harrell, Kyle Page, Droop Pop and Corey Webb connected legacy, entrepreneurship and culture during From Trap to Transformation. A fireside chat between Dr. Beast and hip-hop artist Charly ‘Max B’ Wingate brought another unmistakably cultural moment to the convention before the NECANN Cup closed the stage program.

Elsewhere, Beyond the Booth looked at events as engines for community, sponsorship and revenue. Sessions on therapeutic gardening, cannabis banking and cash operations, consumer wellness experiences, and trust-based retail added practical depth. From 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., Blaze Responsibly's free expungement clinic offered direct help for people with cannabis-related convictions—a reminder that progress in the legal market must also address the continuing impact of prohibition.

Saturday Programming at a Glance

Young Leaders Leveraging Personal Branding and Digital Media — Queenee Gonzalez, Sativa Papi, Audris B. Torres and Toast Vargas

Built for the Block: Brand Identity in New Jersey's Cannabis Market — John Brody, Dharsh Casinathen, Joshua Krane and Tenisha Victor

Drink the Plant: Health, Wellness, Public Policy and Cannabis Beverages — Leo Bridgewater, Matthew Lovett, Wesley McWhite and Reggie ‘Redman’ Noble

From Trap to Transformation — Brandi Hester-Harrell, Kyle Page, Droop Pop and Corey Webb

Beyond the Booth: How Cannabis Events Build Community, Revenue and Growth — Beth Conway, Adelia Fakhri, Ali Fakhri and Ayanna Lawson

Therapeutic Gardening as Harm Reduction for the New Jersey Cannabis Patient — Michael Brennan

Fireside Chat with Max B — Dr. Beast and Charly ‘Max B’ Wingate

Building the Cannabis Back Office: Banking, Cash and Operational Strategy — Susan Crum, Jennifer Makris, Peter Su and Matt Wells

How Cannabis Consumers Are Redefining Community, Self-Care and Social Experiences — Alishea Kelly

NECANN Cup Awards

Adrianna Bauldock took WAJ inside the conversation

A convention this large can become a blur of banners and business cards. Adrianna Bauldock helped slow the weekend down by asking the people behind the booths, brands and programming to explain what they are building and why it matters. Her interviews gave speakers space to expand on their expertise, gave vendors a platform beyond a quick product shot, and gave guests a chance to describe NECANN from the attendee perspective.

That is where WAJ's role as a media partner mattered most. Our coverage was not limited to the biggest name or busiest booth. We looked for the people creating solutions, pushing the culture forward and making room for others in New Jersey's cannabis industry. Watch the embedded interviews throughout this recap and the full VLOG for conversations from the convention floor.

The bigger takeaway for New Jersey cannabis

NECANN New Jersey 2026 made one point clear: the industry is no longer having only one conversation. Regulation still matters, but so do energy costs, banking, workforce development, science, patient education, brand identity, social equity, content, events and customer trust. A company can have a license and still need the right story, the right systems and the right community relationships to last.

The weekend also showed why local media matters. New Jersey's cannabis story should be documented by outlets that understand the state's cities, culture, entrepreneurs and audiences. Through our partnership with Beast Media, We Are Jersey was able to capture not just what happened at NECANN, but how the convention felt: ambitious, candid, educational, relationship-driven and unmistakably Jersey.

If you missed this year's convention, the VLOG and interviews will take you onto the floor. If you attended, consider this your invitation to reconnect with the people you met, follow up on the ideas you heard and keep the conversation moving long after Atlantic City.

Watch and connect: Embed the full NECANN 2026 VLOG here, then link viewers to the We Are Jersey YouTube channel, @WAJMagazine and @WeAreJerseyEnt for additional interviews and New Jersey culture coverage.

posts.title: Maithili Raelle Is Turning Self-Love Into Her Next R&B Chapter
posts.author: Minnee Martinez
posts.summary: R&B has always had a way of making personal experiences feel universal. For Maithili Raelle, that connection between personal growth and music continues to shape her emergence as one of R&B's rising voices.
posts.content:
R&B has always had a way of making personal experiences feel universal. A breakup becomes a ballad. A realization becomes an anthem. A difficult chapter becomes the song somebody else needed to hear. For Maithili Raelle, that connection between personal growth and music continues to shape her emergence as one of R&B's rising voices. The 22-year-old New Jersey-raised artist is stepping into her next chapter with “I Choose Me,” featuring Hiii Siddity, a soulful new release centered around self-worth, independence and the importance of choosing yourself. But for Maithili, choosing yourself isn't necessarily about shutting the world out. It's about finally listening to yourself. 

A Different Kind Of R&B Love Story Maithili's latest release follows the momentum of “Used To Love,” her breakout single that sampled Usher's “You Remind Me” and surpassed 350,000 streams. That record introduced listeners to her ability to pair soulful vocals with emotionally driven storytelling. “I Choose Me” builds on that foundation, but the perspective has changed. This time, the conversation isn't primarily about what happened with someone else. It's about what happens when you decide to prioritize yourself. 

Whether that means walking away from something that no longer feels right, setting boundaries, reclaiming your confidence or simply protecting your peace, “I Choose Me” captures a feeling that has become increasingly familiar to a generation navigating relationships, identity and personal growth in real time. And that's where Maithili's approach becomes especially relatable. She isn't presenting self-love as a perfect destination. She's presenting it as a decision. From Inspiration To Identity Maithili's journey also reflects a larger story happening throughout contemporary R&B: emerging artists are pulling from the records and artists that influenced them while simultaneously creating something unmistakably personal. Her connection to Usher's catalog through “Used To Love” offered listeners a familiar point of entry. But “I Choose Me” makes it clear that Maithili isn't interested in being defined solely by her influences. She's building her own language. Her heritage, experiences and musical influences all become pieces of a larger artistic identity—one that allows her to move between vulnerability, confidence and self-discovery without forcing herself into a single box. That's important for an artist this early in her career. 

At 22, Maithili is still discovering what her sound can become. But there's already a clear throughline in her work: emotion matters. The story matters. And the person behind the voice matters just as much as the record itself. The “I Choose Me” Era There comes a point in every artist's evolution when the music begins to sound less like an introduction and more like a statement. “I Choose Me” feels like that moment for Maithili Raelle. She's not simply following the emotional blueprint of her earlier work. She's expanding it. The result is a record that speaks to anyone who has ever had to make the difficult decision to prioritize their own peace and to anyone still learning that self-worth doesn't require permission. 

From sampling an R&B classic to creating music that speaks directly to her own generation, Maithili is showing that evolution doesn't mean abandoning where you came from. Sometimes it means taking everything you've learned and finally making it yours. With “I Choose Me,” Maithili Raelle isn't just entering another chapter. She's choosing what that chapter gets to sound like. See for yourself here at We Are Jersey Magazine!

posts.title: Latina Civic Foundation Celebrates Latina Excellence, Leadership, and Public Service During Hispanic Heritage Month
posts.author: Manuela Gaviria
posts.summary: As New Jersey celebrates Hispanic Heritage Month and honors the contributions, achievements and leadership of its Latino community, the Latina Civic Foundation will mark a milestone of its own with the inaugural Latina Excellence Breakfast on Friday, October 9, 2026, at The Rutgers Club in Piscataway.
posts.content:
Latina Civic Foundation Celebrates Latina Excellence, Leadership, and Public Service During Hispanic Heritage Month

Featuring New Jersey's First and Second Latina Members of Congress: Congresswoman Nellie Pou and Congresswoman Analilia Mejia
PISCATAWAY, N.J. — September 15, 2026 — As New Jersey celebrates Hispanic Heritage Month and honors the contributions, achievements and leadership of its Latino community, the Latina Civic Foundation will mark a milestone of its own with the inaugural Latina Excellence Breakfast on Friday, October 9, 2026, at The Rutgers Club in Piscataway.

The event celebrates five years of the Latina Civic Foundation and a decade of advancing Latina leadership, civic engagement and public service. The breakfast will feature a historic leadership conversation with Congresswoman Nellie Pou (D-09) and Congresswoman Analilia Mejia (D-11), New Jersey’s first and second Latina members of Congress. Their journeys to Congress mark a significant milestone in New Jersey’s political history and in the growing civic leadership of Latinas across the state.

The Latina Civic Foundation will also honor Zulima Farber, Esq., New Jersey’s first Latina Attorney General, the first female partner at the prestigious law firm Lowenstein Sandler, LLP., and a co-founder of the Latina Civic Foundation. Farber’s groundbreaking career and commitment to public service helped pave the way for generations of Latina leaders across New Jersey and beyond. 

This event will also honor other New Jersey women leaders in public service who became firsts, “Las Primeras,” women who broke glass ceilings and created new possibilities for future generations. Among them are M. Teresa Ruiz, Senate Majority Leader for District 29; Annette Quijano, Speaker Pro-Tempore for District 20; Wilda Diaz, former Mayor of Perth Amboy; Yolanda Garcia-Balicki, Cumberland County Commissioner; and Silvia Catalan-Culnan, Deputy Mayor of Mount Laurel Township. Their trailblazing legacies embody the spirit of Latina Excellence.
“During Hispanic Heritage Month, we celebrate not only where we come from, but also the extraordinary contributions Latinas are making today and the future we are building together,” said María Del Cid-Kosso, Chair of Latina Civic Foundation. “The Latina Excellence Breakfast is an opportunity to honor the women who have broken barriers, created pathways for others, and demonstrated that our voices belong in every room where decisions are made. We are proud to celebrate this legacy while investing in the next generation of Latina leaders.”

"I spend my days in the rooms where policy is written, and I know what changes when a Latina is at that table, and what gets missed when she isn't," said Erika J. Nava, Vice Chair of the Latina Civic Foundation. "Las Primeras opened those doors. Our job now is to make sure the women coming behind them never have to open them alone."

Latina Civic Foundation is a nonprofit educational organization dedicated to advancing Latina leadership through its educational programs, ELLA Wins, Latinas Building the Bench, and the Zulima Farber Cívica Academy. This celebration is made possible by the generous support of national partner organizations, including UnidosUS Action Fund and Latino Victory Foundation, with Univision serving as the celebration's founding corporate media sponsor.

The Latina Civic Foundation’s five-year milestone comes as New Jersey’s Latino community continues to play an increasingly important role in the state’s civic, economic and political life. Yet, according to Center for American Women in Politics (CAWP) Latina representation  in New Jersey still lags behind at 5% of leaders across state and local government agencies and elected positions. The Latina Civic Foundation works in partnership with women organizations to shatter this statistic and advance women leadership in all aspects of public life.

To purchase sponsorships or tickets, visit latinacivicfoundation.org. For questions, reach out to sponsorship@latinacivicfoundation.org.

ABOUT LATINA CIVIC FOUNDATION

Latina Civic Foundation is a 501c3 non-partisan educational committee whose mission is to build a network of civic engagement that expands Latina women’s capacity to develop their leadership potential and impact policy change via civic engagement and public service.

posts.title: Black Fashion in 2026: The Designers, Trends, and Creatives Setting the Agenda
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Black designers and stylists are reshaping luxury, streetwear, and contemporary fashion from the inside out. Here are the names and trends defining Black fashion in 2026.
posts.content:
Fashion has always told you something about who holds cultural power. In 2026, the people setting the agenda in fashion — from the runways of Paris to the streets of Atlanta and Newark — are Black.

That is not a trend. It is a reckoning.

The Runway Is Catching Up to the Street

For decades, fashion institutions benefited from Black culture without compensating or crediting Black creators. The colors, the silhouettes, the references — elements that originated in Black neighborhoods, Black music, and Black creative expression — would cycle through luxury fashion with the origins stripped out.

What is different now is that Black designers are in the rooms where the decisions are made, and they are making different decisions. The 2026 Denim Tears Fall/Winter collection — described as a powerful tribute weaving Black cultural history and luxury fashion — is one example of Black designers using the tools of high fashion to tell Black stories. Not interpreting them from the outside. Owning them.

Streetwear's Second Evolution

The first evolution of streetwear was about making it respectable to mainstream fashion. The second evolution — happening right now — is about taking it back.

Black designers like Freddie Estelle's Durrell Dupard are building brands that exist in the space between streetwear and luxury, refusing to choose between cultural authenticity and craftsmanship. The pieces command attention on red carpets and at community events alike, which is exactly the point.

The Modern Prep Belongs to Us Now

The preppy aesthetic's 2025-2026 renaissance is being rewritten by Black creatives. Ralph Lauren's Oak Bluffs collection, which paid homage to the Black families of Martha's Vineyard, and the way artists like Doechii have injected preppy silhouettes with vibrant, boundary-pushing energy — these are examples of a tradition being reclaimed and expanded.

The Business Side

Fashion is not just aesthetics. It is economics. Black fashion brands are building businesses that challenge the industry's historic underinvestment in Black creative ventures. They are doing it through community-supported launches, direct-to-consumer models, and cross-platform strategies that build audiences before they build collections.

The result is a new kind of fashion brand: one that does not depend on a department store's goodwill or a venture capitalist's timeline. One that belongs to the community that created it.

That is the most important fashion trend of 2026. Not a color, not a silhouette. Ownership.

posts.title: How to Start an Independent Magazine: What 12 Years of WAJ Magazine Has Taught Us
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: WAJ Magazine was founded in 2014 with a vision to amplify New Jersey's most compelling voices. Twelve years and 42+ issues later, here are the lessons that kept us going.
posts.content:
Starting a magazine in 2014 was not the obvious move. Digital media was eating print alive, major publications were cutting staff, and the conventional wisdom said that independent print publishing was a romantic idea with terrible economics.

We started WAJ Magazine anyway.

Twelve years and 42 issues later, we are still here — with a new website, a native blog, a growing national audience, and a community of readers, cover subjects, and contributors who have made this magazine what it is. Here is what we learned along the way.

Start With a Why That Is Bigger Than a Business

WAJ Magazine exists because Bridget Papino and Daniel Banks looked around Bergen County, New Jersey and saw stories that were not being told. Creatives doing extraordinary work. Entrepreneurs building real businesses. Community leaders fighting real fights. Athletes carrying the weight of their neighborhoods. All of them deserving a platform that would tell their stories with the depth and dignity they deserved.

That why has kept us going through every challenge. When a business case is unclear, the mission carries you. Know your mission before you know anything else.

Your Community Is Your Business Model

We have never had a venture capital check. We have never relied on a major media company's infrastructure. What we have is a community of people who believe in what we do — cover subjects who share their features, readers who buy our issues, advertisers who want access to our audience because they know it is real and loyal.

The community is the business model. Every decision we make is filtered through one question: does this serve the people we exist to serve? When the answer is yes, the business tends to take care of itself.

Consistency Over Perfection

Issue 001 of WAJ Magazine was not as good as Issue 042. That is exactly how it is supposed to work. The mistake most people make when starting a creative project is waiting until it is perfect before sharing it with the world.

We put it out. We improved. We put it out again. Forty-two times. The magazine you see today is the result of 12 years of consistent iteration, not a single moment of inspiration.

Own Your Relationships

The cover subjects who have graced our pages are not just editorial decisions. They are relationships — real relationships built on mutual respect, genuine storytelling, and a commitment to representing people accurately and fully. Those relationships are the foundation of everything.

A magazine is only as strong as the trust it has built with the people it covers. Build that trust carefully, and never sacrifice it for a headline.

The Independent Route Is Hard and Worth It

We could have sold. We could have become part of a larger media company's portfolio. We chose not to, because independence means we control the narrative, we choose our cover subjects on merit, and we serve our community without interference.

That independence is expensive sometimes. It is also the thing we are most proud of.

posts.title: The Creator Economy in 2026: How Black Creatives Are Monetizing Their Culture on Their Own Terms
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Black creative entrepreneurs direct a multimedia operation spanning podcast production, music, fashion photography, merchandise, digital analytics, and fulfillment. Created for WAJ Magazine’s examination of the Black creator economy in 2026.
posts.content:
Black creators built the internet. That is not hyperbole — it is increasingly documented history.

The dances that went viral on TikTok, the slang that moved from Black Twitter into mainstream advertising copy, the aesthetic trends that showed up in global fashion campaigns within months of appearing on Black Instagram pages — the cultural pipeline runs in one direction. Black creatives create. Everyone else follows.

What has changed in 2026 is who captures the economic value of that creation.

The Monetization Gap Is Closing

For years, the pattern was familiar and frustrating: Black creators would build something, it would go viral, it would shape culture, and the financial benefit would accrue to platforms, brands, and non-Black artists who adopted the trend. The original creators were left with views, follows, and little else.

The creator economy's maturation has disrupted that pattern — partially. Platforms have built monetization tools. Brand partnerships have become more accessible. Direct-to-fan revenue models through Patreon, Substack, and similar platforms have allowed creators to bypass the intermediaries entirely.

The Black creators who have figured this out are building real businesses. Not influencer deals that depend on a brand's quarterly priorities. Real businesses with multiple revenue streams, owned platforms, and audiences that pay directly because they genuinely want what the creator makes.

What the Smart Ones Are Doing

The most sophisticated Black creators in 2026 treat their cultural fluency as a competitive advantage and protect it accordingly. They know that their audience's loyalty is built on authenticity, and they do not sell that loyalty to the highest bidder.

They diversify. Music plus merchandise plus live events plus online courses plus brand partnerships with companies that actually align with their values. Each stream is smaller than any single deal would be, but together they create a business that no single brand can threaten by pulling a contract.

They own their platforms. Email lists, community apps, private groups — the owned audience is the one that matters. Social media followings are borrowed. The people who gave you their email address chose you specifically.

The Cultural Tax Is Real

Black creators still face a tax that their non-Black counterparts do not. Algorithmic suppression, underpayment relative to reach, brand deals that come with lower rates for the same audience size — these are documented patterns, not paranoia.

The response is not to wait for platforms to fix themselves. The response is to build ownership structures that do not depend on anyone else's fairness. The creators doing this are not naive — they understand the system they are operating in. They are simply building around it.

posts.title: How to Submit Your Music to Magazines and Blogs: A Real Guide for Independent Artists
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Most independent artists approach music press wrong. Here is a practical guide to getting coverage — from crafting a pitch that editors actually read to understanding what publications are really looking for.
posts.content:
Music press coverage is one of the most powerful tools available to an independent artist, and most independent artists have absolutely no idea how to get it.

The problem is not access. The problem is approach. Most artists send the same generic press release to fifty publications and wonder why no one responds. Here is what actually works.

**Research Before You Pitch**

Start with publications that cover your genre and your size. A blog that covers emerging independent artists is a more realistic and useful target than a national magazine that exclusively covers established acts. The goal is to find publications where your story makes sense — where you are neither too big nor too small, and where the publication's existing audience would genuinely be interested in your music.

WAJ Magazine covers artists with a connection to New Jersey and the communities we serve. Pitching us without that connection, regardless of your talent level, is not the right fit. Understanding a publication's focus before reaching out is the most basic and most frequently skipped step in the process.

**Your EPK Has to Work**

An Electronic Press Kit (EPK) is the basic document you send to any media contact. It needs to include: a short bio (two to three paragraphs maximum), your best press photo at high resolution, links to your music, any previous press coverage, contact information, and social media handles with current follower counts.

What it should not include: a generic "about me" written in third person that reads like it was written by committee, a photo taken in bad lighting with a phone camera, or links to a SoundCloud page you have not updated in two years.

Your EPK represents your professionalism before your music does. Make it reflect the level of attention you put into your art.

**The Pitch Email**

Keep it short. Three to four sentences maximum. Who you are, what you make, why it is relevant to this specific publication, and a link to listen. That is it.

Editors receive dozens of pitches a day. The ones that get opened are the ones that clearly understand the publication, get to the point quickly, and make it easy to say yes.

**Follow Up Once**

If you do not hear back within two weeks, one polite follow-up is appropriate. One. If there is still no response, move on. Repeated follow-ups do not demonstrate persistence — they demonstrate an inability to read a room.

**Be Ready When It Works**

When a publication says yes, have everything ready. High-resolution photos, a full bio, links to your music in multiple formats. The faster you can turn around professional materials, the better the coverage will be and the better the relationship with that publication becomes going forward.

Press coverage is a relationship game. The first placement leads to the second. Treat every editor like the long-term relationship they could become.

posts.title: The Best Podcasts by Black Creators You Need in Your Rotation Right Now

posts.summary: Black podcast creators are producing some of the most thoughtful, entertaining, and culturally significant audio content available today. Here are the shows that deserve your ears in 2026.

Podcasting in 2026 is both oversaturated and full of genuine gems. The challenge is not finding something to listen to — it is finding something worth giving your time and attention to consistently.

Black podcast creators have been doing something interesting throughout the medium's evolution: building audiences before the platforms caught up, creating niche communities around specific cultural conversations, and demonstrating that authentic storytelling does not need a major media company behind it to find the people it was meant for.

If you are building something, these voices will tell you things that more mainstream business media will not.

The rise of Black podcasters is part of a larger pattern: when the gatekeeping of traditional media did not make room, creators built their own rooms. And the audiences that filled those rooms were larger than anyone on the traditional side expected.

That is the pattern. It repeats. Pay attention to where it goes next.

posts.title: How Hip-Hop Became the Most Influential Genre in the World — And What Comes Next
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Hip-hop is 50+ years old and still the most culturally dominant genre on the planet. Here is how it got there, what it has built, and where it is going next.
posts.content:
Hip-hop is the most influential genre in the history of recorded music. Not the most commercially successful genre in any single year. Not the most critically lauded. The most influential — full stop.

To understand why requires looking at what influence actually means in music. Influence is not about how many albums are sold in a quarter. It is about how many other genres, artists, fashion movements, linguistic trends, business models, and cultural frameworks have been shaped by a single creative tradition.

By that measure, nothing comes close.

**Where It Started**

The South Bronx, 1973. A DJ named Kool Herc extended the percussion break in a record by isolating and looping it — creating the foundation for an entirely new relationship between the crowd and the music. What happened in that room was not just the birth of a genre. It was the birth of a completely new creative methodology: sampling, remixing, building something new from the raw material of what came before.

That methodology became foundational not just to hip-hop but to electronic music, pop production, and almost every genre that followed.

**What It Built**

Hip-hop did not just create music. It created an entire cultural ecosystem. Fashion, language, visual art, dance, film, television, entrepreneurship — every element of the culture developed its own vocabulary, its own industry, and its own economy. The genre that corporate America dismissed as a trend in the 1980s became the dominant commercial force in American culture by the 2000s and the dominant global force by the 2010s.

The recognition of Dr. Dre at the 2026 American Music Honors — the first hip-hop artist to receive the distinction — is a reminder of how long it took institutions to catch up to what people already knew.

**Where It Is Going**

Hip-hop in 2026 is in an interesting position. The genre is so dominant that younger artists are pushing against its conventions, blending it with R&B, Afrobeats, reggaeton, and electronic music in ways that make genre labels feel inadequate. The next evolution of hip-hop is already happening — it just has not been named yet.

What will not change is the methodology: sampling the past, building in the present, and creating the template for what comes next. That is what hip-hop has always done.

And it will keep doing it.

posts.title: How to Get Featured in a Magazine: A Complete Guide for NJ Creatives
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Getting featured in a magazine is one of the most powerful credibility moves a creative, entrepreneur, or community leader can make. Here is exactly how to approach it — and what WAJ Magazine's editorial team looks for.
posts.content:
Getting featured in a magazine is one of the most powerful credibility moves a creative, entrepreneur, athlete, or community leader can make. A magazine feature is a third-party endorsement that says: this person's story is worth stopping for. It opens doors, builds authority, and creates content that lives far beyond the news cycle.

But most people do not know how to pursue it, and the ones who do often go about it the wrong way. Here is what actually works.

**Start with the Right Fit**

The biggest mistake people make is pitching everywhere at once without thinking about fit. A fashion-forward lifestyle magazine is not the right home for a story about community organizing, even if the community organizer is stylish. A regional magazine like WAJ Magazine is not the right home for a story with no connection to New Jersey or the communities we cover.

Read the publication before you pitch it. Understand who they feature, what tone they use, and what kind of stories they have told before. Your pitch should feel like it belongs in that publication — not like it was copied and pasted from a press kit.

**Lead with Your Story, Not Your Résumé**

Editors do not want a list of your accomplishments. They want a story. What have you been through? What are you building? What problem are you solving? What does your journey reveal about something larger than yourself?

Your résumé tells an editor what you have done. Your story tells them why it matters. Lead with the story.

**Have a Clear Angle**

"I'm a musician from New Jersey" is not an angle. "I grew up in Irvington, turned down a Division I basketball scholarship to pursue music, and just released my first independent album funded entirely by community pre-sales" — that is an angle.

The more specific you are, the more compelling your pitch becomes. Specificity is not limiting. It is what makes a story feel real.

**How to Pitch WAJ Magazine**

Our submission process is straightforward and free. Go to wajmagazine.com/features and fill out the form with your story, your background, and why you believe your voice belongs in WAJ Magazine. We read every submission personally and respond within 30 days if you are selected.

We do not charge for features. We do not accept payment for placement. Every feature in WAJ Magazine is selected on merit because we believe that is the only way to preserve the integrity of what we do.

**After the Feature**

A magazine feature is only as powerful as what you do with it after it runs. Share it on your social platforms. Link to it from your website. Include it in your press kit. Send it to potential partners and collaborators. A well-placed feature can open conversations that last for years — but only if you use it.

Your story deserves to be told. The question is whether you are willing to tell it.

posts.title: How to Grow Your Brand as a Creative Entrepreneur in 2026
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: The creator economy has matured. In 2026, building a sustainable brand as a creative entrepreneur requires more than a following — it requires strategy, consistency, and a clear value proposition.
posts.content:
Everyone wants to be a brand. Not everyone is willing to do what building one actually requires.

In 2026, the creator economy is not in its infancy anymore. There are millions of people competing for attention across every platform, in every niche, with every tool available. The ones who are building real, sustainable businesses are not doing something magical. They are doing something disciplined.

**Know What You Are Actually Selling**

This is the first question most creative entrepreneurs skip, and it is the most important one. A photographer is not selling photos. A musician is not selling songs. A personal stylist is not selling outfits.

You are selling a feeling, an outcome, or a transformation. The photographer sells the way it feels to have your most important moments preserved beautifully. The musician sells the experience of hearing something that makes a listener feel understood. The stylist sells confidence and the freedom of not having to think about getting dressed.

When you know what you are actually selling, your marketing becomes simple. You talk about the feeling, the outcome, the transformation. The product is just how you deliver it.

**Build in Public**

The era of the mysterious, inaccessible brand is largely over for independent creatives. Audiences want to see the process. They want to see the work in progress, the failures, the behind-the-scenes reality. Sharing your journey in real time builds trust at a pace that polished content rarely matches.

This does not mean oversharing. It means letting people into the parts of your process that are genuinely interesting — the creative decisions, the obstacles you are navigating, the lessons you are learning in real time.

**Monetize the Community Before You Monetize the Content**

The mistake most creators make is building an audience and then trying to sell to it. The smarter move is to build a community with a shared interest or identity, and then create products and experiences that serve that community's specific needs.

A community buys because they believe in what you are doing and they want to be part of it. An audience buys — sometimes — because the right offer landed at the right moment.

Build the community. The monetization follows.

**Consistency Is the Competitive Advantage**

In a space saturated with people who post for a month and disappear, the single most powerful thing you can do is show up regularly over a long period of time. Not every day. Not with perfect content. Just consistently, with genuine intention, for longer than most people are willing to sustain.

The creative entrepreneurs who are winning in 2026 started three, five, seven years ago and did not stop. They were not overnight successes. They were consistent over time, and consistency compounded.

posts.title: Jersey Club in 2026: How New Jersey's Sound Is Still Running the East Coast
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Jersey Club was born in Newark's club scene and has become one of the most influential sounds in electronic music globally. In 2026, the genre is bigger than ever — and it still belongs to New Jersey.
posts.content:
There are music genres that come from places. Then there are music genres that ARE places. Jersey Club is the second kind.

Born in Newark's late-night club scene in the early 2000s, Jersey Club is a percussion-driven, high-energy genre built on chopped vocal samples, propulsive kicks, and an energy that is uniquely, unmistakably New Jersey. It moves at around 140 BPM and it does not let up. If you have heard it in a club, at a block party, in someone's car with the windows down on a summer night in Essex County — you know exactly what we are talking about.

In 2026, Jersey Club is not underground anymore. It never really was for people from here. But its global reach has expanded in ways that would have been hard to predict a decade ago. The genre has influenced pop production, been sampled by major artists, and found audiences far outside the tri-state area. DJ Smallz 732 — who graced the cover of WAJ Magazine Issue 041 — is one of the architects who has helped carry the sound forward while keeping it rooted in where it came from.

**What Makes Jersey Club Different**

The genre is technical. The DJ craft behind it is serious. The chopping, the layering, the way energy builds and drops — these are skills developed over years of playing for real audiences in real rooms who will let you know immediately if the vibe is off.

What separates Jersey Club from other regional electronic genres is its community. This is music made by people from specific neighborhoods for people from those neighborhoods. That specificity is not a limitation — it is the source of its power. The more local it is, the more real it feels. And the more real it feels, the further it travels.

**The Next Generation**

Newark, Irvington, East Orange, Jersey City — the pipeline of Jersey Club talent is not slowing down. Younger producers and DJs are building on the foundation laid by pioneers, adding new influences while keeping the percussion and the energy that define the sound.

If you want to understand where music is going, watch where it came from. And right now, a significant part of where music came from is New Jersey.

posts.title: ESSENCE Festival 2026: The Moments That Defined the Weekend and What They Mean
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: ESSENCE Festival 2026 brought Michelle Obama, Cardi B, Missy Elliott, Teyana Taylor, and thousands of Black entrepreneurs together in New Orleans for three days that reminded everyone exactly who drives American culture.
posts.content:
ESSENCE Festival 2026 was not just a concert. It never is.

For three days in New Orleans, the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center and the stages surrounding it became the largest gathering of Black culture, Black business, Black joy, and Black excellence in the country. Michelle Obama, Cardi B, Brandy, Monica, Missy Elliott, Teyana Taylor, and T.I. were among the names that drew the crowds. But the real energy — the thing that makes ESSENCE Festival irreplaceable — happened in between the performances.

It happened in the entrepreneur conversations between strangers who recognized something in each other. In the panels where Black women leaders said things out loud that they are rarely given space to say. In the BeautyCon footprint where a generation of Black beauty founders stood next to their products and talked directly to the customers who built their businesses.

**What Teyana Taylor's Set Said**

Teyana Taylor on the ESSENCE Main Stage as both performer and curator is a statement about range. She is an artist, a creative director, a cultural curator, and a businesswoman — and she holds all of those identities simultaneously without apologizing for any of them. Her presence at ESSENCE was a reminder that the most compelling voices in Black culture are the ones that refuse to be simplified.

**The Business Floor**

ESSENCE Festival's business programming does not get enough credit. While the stages get the attention, some of the most valuable conversations at the festival happen in the convention center — panels on funding, entrepreneurship, media ownership, and wealth building. The people in those rooms are building things that will outlast any single performance.

**Why ESSENCE Festival Matters in 2026**

The cultural and economic power represented at ESSENCE Festival each year is a direct rebuttal to every narrative that tries to minimize Black America's contribution to this country's identity. As one entrepreneur put it during the weekend: Black culture is not standing outside the marketplace waiting to be included. We are the marketplace.

That is the energy ESSENCE Festival carries. It has been carrying it for decades. And in 2026, it has never felt more necessary.

posts.title: The Best Black-Owned Restaurants in Newark, NJ You Need to Try in 2026
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Newark's culinary scene is thriving, and Black-owned restaurants are at the center of it. From soul food institutions to Caribbean kitchens and modern dining concepts, here are the spots defining Newark's food culture right now.
posts.content:
Newark has always fed people — physically, culturally, and spiritually. But in 2026, the city's dining scene is having a moment that deserves more attention than it gets, and Black-owned restaurants are the engine driving it.

These are not hidden gems. They are established businesses, community anchors, and culinary statements made by people who love their craft, love their city, and love the people they feed. Here is a look at some of the Black-owned dining experiences shaping Newark's food culture right now.

**Soul Food and Southern Comfort**

Newark's soul food tradition runs deep. The restaurants carrying that tradition forward are doing it with pride — large portions, family recipes, and the kind of warmth that makes you feel like you are eating at someone's home, because in spirit, you are.
