A newer generation of Black restaurateurs in Newark is bringing elevated concepts to the city without losing connection to the community. Farm-to-table influences, chef-driven menus, and contemporary dining experiences that hold their own against anything in New York City — at a fraction of the cost and with a hundred percent more soul.

**Why Eating Black-Owned in Newark Matters**

Every dollar spent at a Black-owned restaurant in Newark stays closer to the community. It supports a family, it funds a payroll, it pays for a child's school supplies. The multiplier effect of buying local and buying Black is real, and it compounds over time.

Newark has always been a city that gives more than it gets credit for. Its Black-owned restaurants are one of the best examples of that. Go eat. Tell people. Come back.

posts.title: Black-Owned Brands Dominating in 2026 — Without DEI as a Crutch
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: As DEI initiatives fade from corporate focus, Black-owned brands are scaling through innovation, cultural relevance, and strategy that does not depend on anyone else's goodwill.
posts.content:
There are roughly 4.6 million Black-owned businesses in the United States today. That number matters. But what matters more is what is happening inside those businesses — the innovation, the strategy, and the cultural intelligence that is driving growth in an environment that has never fully supported Black entrepreneurship.

In 2026, DEI is no longer the story. The brands that were built on the foundation of someone else's commitment to inclusion are finding out whether they have what it takes to stand on their own. The brands built on product quality, community loyalty, and genuine cultural resonance are thriving.

**The Shift That Was Always Coming**

Corporate DEI spending surged after 2020 and has since retreated significantly. For Black entrepreneurs who built their business strategy around landing in a major retailer's diversity section or securing a brand partnership from a company trying to improve its optics, that retreat has been painful.

But for the entrepreneurs who built real products for real customers who genuinely needed them — the retreat of corporate DEI has barely registered. Their customers were never shopping out of obligation. They were shopping because the product was better.

**What the Winning Brands Have in Common**

The Black-owned brands that are scaling in 2026 share a few consistent traits. They know exactly who their customer is and they speak to that customer directly, without translation. They have a clear cultural point of view that is not performative — it is foundational to the product itself. And they have built community around the brand, not just a customer list.

From hair care to fashion to spirits to food, the template is consistent: deep customer understanding, genuine cultural connection, and a product that performs.

**The Takeaway**

Black entrepreneurship in 2026 is not waiting for permission or support from institutions that have historically withheld both. It is building regardless, because the community it serves is real, the need is real, and the talent doing the building has always been real.

That is not a new story. It is just finally getting the coverage it deserves.

posts.title: American Music Honors 2026: How New Jersey Cemented Its Place as America's Music Capital
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: The 2026 American Music Honors at Monmouth University honored Dr. Dre, Dionne Warwick, Patti Smith, and The E Street Band — cementing New Jersey's undeniable role in shaping American music history.
posts.content:
If there was ever any doubt that New Jersey belongs in the conversation as America's premier music state, the 2026 American Music Honors put it to rest.

Held at Monmouth University's Pollak Theatre in West Long Branch, the fourth annual American Music Honors delivered one of the most genre-spanning, culturally significant ceremonies in the event's short but already impactful history. Hosted by the Bruce Springsteen Center for American Music, this is not a traditional awards show. There are no popular votes, no commercial metrics, and no red carpet theatrics designed for social media. It is a ceremony built around one question: whose contribution to American music has extended beyond charts and into the fabric of American identity?

The 2026 class answered that question with a lineup that will be studied for years.

**Dr. Dre** became the first hip-hop artist in the event's history to receive the honor. The significance of that milestone cannot be overstated. Hip-hop is the most influential music genre of the last 50 years — commercially, culturally, and globally — and its formal recognition at an institution rooted in New Jersey's music legacy represents something overdue and necessary. Dr. Dre's production catalog alone reshaped what popular music sounds like.

**Dionne Warwick**, a Newark native and one of New Jersey's most beloved musical daughters, received recognition that felt personal for the Garden State crowd. Warwick has spent decades as both a recording artist and a cultural ambassador, and her voice remains one of the most distinctive in American music history.

**Patti Smith**, recognized as one of the most influential poetic voices in rock history, and **The E Street Band**, synonymous with the sound of New Jersey itself, rounded out a class that felt both inevitable and electric.

A posthumous tribute to **The Band** added the kind of reverence that only this ceremony seems capable of delivering.

**What This Means for New Jersey**

New Jersey has always known what it contributes to American music. Springsteen, Bon Jovi, Whitney Houston, Queen Latifah, Lauryn Hill, Redman, Fetty Wap, Naughty by Nature — the list of artists who carry the Garden State in their DNA is as long as it is impressive.

The American Music Honors is increasingly becoming the institution that says it out loud. And the fact that it lives in New Jersey — not Nashville, not Los Angeles, not New York — matters. It is a statement about ownership, about where this music comes from, and about who gets to tell that story.

For WAJ Magazine, which has spent 12 years documenting the voices that make New Jersey's culture what it is, the 2026 American Music Honors felt like validation of everything we have always known: this state does not borrow culture. It creates it.

posts.title: How Independent Musicians Are Building Empires Without Major Labels in 2026
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: The music industry has fundamentally shifted. In 2026, independent artists are building sustainable careers, loyal audiences, and real revenue without signing away their creative control.
posts.content:
The major label deal used to be the only path. You either got signed or you stayed local. There was no middle ground, no infrastructure for independence at scale, and no blueprint for building a music career outside of a corporate system that owned your masters and dictated your timeline.

That world is gone. And what has replaced it is something more interesting.

In 2026, independent musicians are building careers that in some cases outperform what labels can offer — on their own terms, with their own ownership, and with a direct relationship to their audiences that no label contract can replicate.

**The Infrastructure Changed**

Distribution platforms like DistroKid, TuneCore, and UnitedMasters have made it possible for any artist to get their music on every major streaming platform globally within 24 hours. No label needed. No gatekeeping.

Social platforms — TikTok, Instagram, YouTube — have replaced radio as the primary discovery mechanism for new music. An artist with a genuine point of view and a consistent presence can build an audience of millions without a publicist, a marketing budget, or a label.

The tools that used to cost hundreds of thousands of dollars now cost almost nothing. A professional-quality recording setup that would have required a major studio in 1995 fits in a laptop bag in 2026.

**The Business Model Shifted**

Independent artists are not just recording and releasing. The smart ones are building businesses. Merchandise. Live events. Brand partnerships. Sync licensing. Fan subscriptions through platforms like Patreon. Online courses teaching other artists the skills they developed. Each revenue stream compounds the others.

The artists who are winning independently in 2026 treat their music like a product and their fanbase like a community. They show up consistently, communicate directly, and build loyalty that no playlist algorithm can manufacture.

**What This Means for You**

If you are an independent artist reading this, the path exists. It is not easy — nothing worth building ever is. But the tools are there, the audience is reachable, and the ownership is available in a way it has never been before.

The major label deal is not the dream anymore. Owning your work is the dream. And in 2026, that dream is more achievable than ever.

posts.title: Jersey City SummerFest 2026: Your Complete Guide to the City's Free Outdoor Concert Series
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Jersey City's iconic SummerFest returns for its 51st season with soul, jazz, funk, R&B, gospel, and more at Liberty State Park and Berry Lane Park — completely free all summer long.
posts.content:
For 51 years, Jersey City's SummerFest has done what very few free events can: it has brought an entire city together through the universal language of music.

The 2026 edition of SummerFest — presented by Mayor James Solomon, the Jersey City Municipal Council, and the Jersey City Office of Cultural Affairs, in partnership with the Jersey City Free Public Library and Liberty State Park — continues that legacy with a season-long lineup that spans soul, jazz, funk, R&B, Latin, Americana, gospel, and more.

What makes SummerFest different from the wave of outdoor concerts that fill every summer calendar is this: it has never charged a ticket price, and it has never compromised on the quality of its performers. Both nationally recognized musicians and top-tier local bands share the same stage, treating the audience with the same respect whether they drove from Manhattan or walked from three blocks away.

**Where and When**

Performances run on a rotating weekly schedule across three outdoor venues:

- **Sundays, 6–8 PM** — North Cove Field (behind the ferry parking lot)
- **Tuesdays, 6:30–8:30 PM** — South Lawn (flag plaza)
- **Thursdays, 6:30–8:30 PM** — Berry Lane Park

The variety of locations matters. North Cove Field puts you right on the waterfront with Manhattan as your backdrop. Berry Lane Park brings the concert to one of Jersey City's most community-centered green spaces. There is no bad seat at any of them.

**Why SummerFest Matters Beyond the Music**

Free concert series are often treated as pleasant background noise — something to walk through with a cup of coffee. SummerFest is not that. It is a genuine cultural institution that has watched Jersey City change around it for five decades and remained a constant point of connection across neighborhoods, generations, and backgrounds.

In a city that has undergone significant gentrification pressure over the past decade, SummerFest represents something worth protecting: public space, public culture, and public access. The fact that it is still free, still local, and still filled with people who genuinely love music is not an accident. It is the result of intentional community investment.

**How to Make the Most of It**

Arrive 15–20 minutes early for good positioning, especially at North Cove where the waterfront views are premium. Bring a blanket or lawn chair — seating is general admission and the grass fills up quickly on warm evenings. Food vendors are typically on-site, but the local restaurant scene around each venue is worth exploring before or after the show.

Follow the Jersey City Office of Cultural Affairs on social media for real-time lineup updates — acts are added throughout the season and the best performances are often announced with short notice.

SummerFest is one of the best things happening in New Jersey this summer. It always has been.

posts.title: How to Find and Support Black-Owned Businesses in New Jersey
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: New Jersey is home to thousands of Black-owned businesses across every industry — restaurants, salons, boutiques, tech firms, and more. Here's how to find them, support them year-round, and why it matters more than ever.
posts.content:
Supporting Black-owned businesses is one of the most direct and immediate ways to invest in your community. Every dollar you spend with a Black-owned business in New Jersey creates a ripple effect — it funds a payroll, pays a lease, covers a child's school expenses, and contributes to building generational wealth in communities that have historically been denied it.

New Jersey has a remarkable ecosystem of Black-owned businesses. From Newark's growing restaurant scene to Bergen County's boutique retail, from Trenton's creative studios to Jersey City's tech startups, Black entrepreneurs are building real businesses that serve real needs — and they need real customers.

**How to Find Black-Owned Businesses in New Jersey**

Several directories make it easier to find and support Black-owned businesses in the state. The New Jersey Black Chamber of Commerce maintains an active directory of member businesses across categories including retail, food service, professional services, construction, and technology. The Official Black Wall Street app and directory also lists thousands of Black-owned businesses nationally, with strong New Jersey representation. Local Facebook groups, Instagram hashtags like #BlackOwnedNJ and #NJBlackBusiness, and community organizations like the Urban League of Essex County all maintain updated lists.

**Why Shopping Local and Black Matters**

Research consistently shows that money spent at Black-owned businesses has a higher economic multiplier effect within Black communities than spending at large corporations. When you eat at a Black-owned restaurant in Newark, buy from a Black-owned boutique in Montclair, or hire a Black-owned contractor in Camden, a larger percentage of that money stays within the community — recirculating through local suppliers, local employees, and local families.

The racial wealth gap in New Jersey is among the worst in the country, with white families holding a median household wealth of $662,500 compared to under $20,000 for Black and Latino families. One of the most direct and personal ways to push back against that gap is to redirect your spending toward businesses owned by people who have been structurally excluded from building wealth.

**Go Beyond Food**

The most common form of supporting Black-owned businesses is visiting restaurants — and that matters. But the impact goes deeper when you expand your support across categories. Hire a Black-owned accountant, attorney, or financial advisor. Choose a Black-owned cleaning service, landscaping company, or contractor for your home. Shop at Black-owned bookstores, clothing boutiques, and beauty supply stores. Purchase from Black-owned tech companies, marketing agencies, and event planners.

The goal is to make Black-owned businesses part of your regular rotation, not just a February ritual.

**Amplify What You Find**

When you have a great experience at a Black-owned business, say so publicly. Leave a Google review. Share on Instagram. Tell your friends and colleagues. Word of mouth is still one of the most powerful marketing tools a small business has — and it costs you nothing.

WAJ Magazine has been featuring New Jersey's Black-owned businesses and entrepreneurs since 2014. If you own or know a business that deserves a spotlight, submit it at wajmagazine.com/features.

posts.title: New Jersey Real Estate Market 2026: What Buyers, Sellers & Renters Need to Know
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: New Jersey's real estate market in 2026 remains competitive, expensive, and evolving. Whether you're trying to buy your first home, sell at the right time, or navigate a tough rental market, here's what you need to know right now.
posts.content:
New Jersey's real estate market has not gotten easier to navigate. Prices remain elevated across most of the state, inventory continues to be a challenge, and the rental market has not offered much relief. But there are shifts happening in 2026 that buyers, sellers, and renters all need to understand.

**The Buying Landscape**

For buyers, 2026 has brought some relief on mortgage rates compared to the peak years, but affordability remains a serious challenge. New Jersey consistently ranks among the most expensive states in the country for homeownership, and the gap between home prices and median household incomes — particularly in Black and Latino communities — remains wide.

First-time homebuyers should know that the New Jersey Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency (HMFA) continues to offer programs specifically designed to help, including down payment assistance, competitive fixed-rate mortgages, and homebuyer education requirements that prepare buyers for what ownership actually involves. These programs are underutilized and worth exploring before assuming you cannot afford to buy.

Location is everything in New Jersey right now. The communities that were considered affordable alternatives a few years ago — parts of Essex County, Hudson County, and South Jersey — have themselves experienced significant price appreciation. Understanding which neighborhoods are still accessible and which have moved out of reach requires working with someone who knows local market conditions.

**The Selling Window**

For sellers, the market in most of New Jersey remains favorable. Inventory is still relatively low in most price ranges, which means well-priced homes in desirable locations continue to move quickly and often above asking price. The key word is "well-priced" — overpriced homes are now sitting longer as buyers have become more selective.

If you are considering selling, the strategic question is not just whether to sell but what to do next. Many potential sellers are staying put because they bought or refinanced at low rates and do not want to enter the buyer's market they would have to navigate after selling. This "lock-in effect" continues to constrain supply and prop up prices.

**Renters Facing Real Pressure**

The rental market in New Jersey is extremely challenging. Rent increases over the past three years have outpaced income growth significantly, and vacancy rates remain low in urban centers. Newark, Jersey City, Hoboken, and the suburbs surrounding them have seen rental prices reach levels that many long-term residents simply cannot sustain.

Several municipalities have taken steps to expand renter protections, but the fundamental supply problem — New Jersey has not built enough housing to meet demand for decades — remains unresolved. Renters who are able to qualify for homeownership programs should strongly consider making the transition, as the monthly cost difference between renting and owning is narrowing in many parts of the state.

**The Bottom Line**

New Jersey's real estate market in 2026 rewards preparation, patience, and local knowledge. Whether you are buying, selling, or renting, understand your options, know the resources available to you, and work with professionals who understand the communities you are targeting.

posts.title: Jersey Club 101: The History and Sound of Newark's Signature Genre
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Jersey Club is Newark's gift to the world. Born in the city's late-night club scene, it has grown into a globally recognized genre that still belongs to New Jersey. Here's everything you need to know about where it came from and why it matters.
posts.content:
If you have ever heard a DJ drop a track that made the entire room lose their minds before you could even identify the song, there is a good chance you were listening to Jersey Club.

Jersey Club is a percussion-driven, high-energy genre of electronic dance music that originated in Newark, New Jersey in the late 1990s and early 2000s. It is built on chopped vocal samples, propulsive kick patterns, hi-hat rolls, and a tempo that typically runs around 130-140 BPM. When it hits right, it is impossible not to move.

**Where It Came From**

The genre's roots are in the house music and hip-hop culture that defined Newark's club scene for decades. DJs in Newark's underground clubs began developing a distinctive sound — taking elements of Baltimore Club (itself a descendant of Chicago House) and mixing them with hip-hop production sensibilities and a uniquely Jersey energy.

The vocal chopping technique — where vocal samples are cut, reversed, and layered into percussive rhythms — became the genre's most distinctive calling card. A voice becomes a drum. A phrase becomes a groove. The result is something that operates at a different frequency than almost anything else in electronic music.

DJs like DJ Tameil, DJ Smallz 732, Tim Dolla, and others helped develop and popularize the sound through mixtapes, club nights, and early internet distribution, building a genre from the ground up without major label support or mainstream radio play.

**The Sound Defined**

What makes Jersey Club immediately recognizable to anyone who has heard it:

The kick pattern is unconventional. Where most dance music lands the kick on predictable beats, Jersey Club kicks dance around the grid, creating a syncopated energy that keeps the listener slightly off-balance in the best possible way.

The vocal chops are specific. Three-syllable phrases are the genre's lingua franca — "Oh my God," "what happened," "do it" — chopped and looped until the words stop meaning anything and start functioning as pure rhythm.

The energy is relentless. Jersey Club tracks do not build toward a drop in the traditional electronic music sense. The entire track is the drop. There is nowhere to rest.

**How Far It Has Traveled**

Jersey Club is no longer just a Newark phenomenon. The genre has influenced pop production, been sampled by Grammy-winning artists, found dedicated audiences across the globe, and generated academic interest as a case study in how regional music travels through digital networks.

When Cardi B incorporated Jersey Club elements, when global DJs started programming Jersey Club tracks into international sets, when music critics began writing seriously about the genre — Newark DJs were still the ones who invented it, still the ones who live it.

**WAJ Magazine and Jersey Club**

WAJ Magazine has covered Jersey Club artists and culture since our early issues. DJ Smallz 732, one of the genre's key figures, graced the cover of Issue 041. The culture we document and the culture that produced Jersey Club are the same culture — Newark, New Jersey, doing what it has always done: creating something out of nothing and sharing it with the world.

posts.title: How to Start a Small Business in New Jersey (2026 Guide)
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Starting a business in New Jersey in 2026 is more accessible than ever — but the steps matter. From registering your business to finding funding, here is a practical guide built for NJ entrepreneurs.
posts.content:
New Jersey is one of the best states in the country to start a business. It is also one of the most expensive. Understanding what you are getting into — and how to navigate the process strategically — can be the difference between a business that struggles through its first year and one that builds momentum from day one.

**Step 1: Choose Your Business Structure**

Before you can register your business in New Jersey, you need to decide what legal structure makes sense. The most common options for small business owners are:

Sole Proprietorship — simplest to set up, no formal registration required, but offers no personal liability protection. Your personal assets are on the line if your business is sued.

LLC (Limited Liability Company) — the most popular structure for small businesses in New Jersey. It provides liability protection, is relatively inexpensive to form, and offers tax flexibility. Most small businesses should start as an LLC.

Corporation — more complex and expensive to maintain, but may be appropriate if you plan to raise investment capital or have multiple shareholders.

For most first-time entrepreneurs, an LLC is the right starting point. Formation costs in New Jersey run approximately $125 in state filing fees.

**Step 2: Register with the State**

To formally register your LLC or corporation in New Jersey, file with the New Jersey Division of Revenue and Enterprise Services at njportal.com/DOR/BusinessFormation. You will need to choose a registered agent (a person or company that receives legal documents on behalf of your business), select your business name, and pay the filing fee.

Once registered, you will receive a New Jersey Business Registration Certificate, which you will need to open a business bank account and apply for permits and licenses.

**Step 3: Get Your EIN**

An Employer Identification Number (EIN) is your business's federal tax ID. You apply for one free of charge at irs.gov, and it takes about ten minutes. You will need this for your business bank account, tax filings, and if you ever hire employees.

**Step 4: Understand Your Licensing Requirements**

New Jersey licensing requirements vary significantly by industry. Restaurants, contractors, healthcare providers, childcare facilities, and many other businesses require state or local licenses. The New Jersey Business Action Center (business.nj.gov) is the best resource for understanding exactly what your specific business needs.

**Step 5: Separate Your Finances**

Open a business checking account as soon as your business is legally registered. Never mix personal and business finances — this is one of the most common mistakes new entrepreneurs make, and it creates accounting nightmares and can undermine the liability protection your LLC is supposed to provide.

**Step 6: Find Funding**

New Jersey has a strong network of small business funding resources. The New Jersey Economic Development Authority (NJEDA) offers grants, loans, and tax incentives specifically for NJ businesses. SCORE NJ provides free mentoring from experienced business professionals. The New Jersey Small Business Development Centers (NJSBDCs) offer free consulting and low-cost training.

Black entrepreneurs should also explore the New Jersey Black Chamber of Commerce and organizations like the Urban League of Essex County and New Jersey Institute for Social Justice, which offer specific resources and advocacy for minority-owned businesses.

Starting a business is not easy. But in New Jersey in 2026, the resources exist to do it right. The most important step is the first one: decide to start.

posts.title: U.S. Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester, Mayor John Carney, New Castle County Executive Marcus Henry to Open the YDC
posts.author: Desiree P. Bell
posts.summary: U.S. Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester, Mayor John Carney, and New Castle County Executive Marcus Henry joined community leaders to open Wilmington's new $19.3 million Youth Development Center — a 42,000-square-foot hub built for the next generation.
posts.content:
U.S. Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester, Wilmington Mayor John Carney, and New Castle County Executive Marcus Henry joined the Community Education Building (CEB) to mark the grand opening of Wilmington's new Youth Development Center — a $19.3 million, 42,000-square-foot facility built specifically for the young people of Wilmington's East Side.

The Youth Development Center (YDC), located at 315 East 12th Street, represents years of community advocacy, fundraising, and planning. It stands as an extension of the Community Education Building one block away, creating a connected campus designed to support learning, creativity, wellness, and opportunity across all ages.

Senator Blunt Rochester, the first woman and first African American to represent Delaware in both chambers of Congress, had previously toured the center as construction neared completion and called its model "something that could be replicated across the nation." Her appearance at the grand opening alongside the Mayor and County Executive underscored the level of governmental commitment behind the project.

**What the YDC Offers**

The 42,000-square-foot center is built for real use. The facility includes a full gymnasium with a basketball court, a black box theater and performance arts space, smart classrooms, a fitness room, a youth lounge, and — through a partnership with the YMCA of Delaware — an Early Learning Academy offering high-quality early education for up to 100 children from infancy through pre-K.

For Wilmington's East Side, which is home to approximately 5,000 students within the 19801 ZIP code, the YDC represents access to resources that were previously unavailable in the neighborhood.

"What happened at YDC Fest is what this Center is all about — bringing people together around our young people," said Luther Jennings of the Community Education Building. "Friday was a celebration, but it was also a beginning. The doors are now open, and we are excited about what comes next."

**Why This Matters**

Youth development infrastructure — the kind that provides safe spaces, mentorship, athletics, arts programming, and early childhood education — is one of the most direct investments a community can make in its own future. The YDC represents precisely that kind of investment: a physical commitment to the belief that the young people of Wilmington's East Side deserve a place to grow, learn, and belong.

The grand opening is a beginning, not a conclusion. The real story of the Youth Development Center will be written by the young people who walk through its doors in the years ahead.

posts.title: Pastor Turner Walk 40 Miles from Underground Railroad Site to Trenton, Spotlight Petition Demanding Passage of Two Reparations Bills
posts.author: Bridget Papino
posts.summary: Rev. Dr. Robert Turner completed Walk #46 of his ongoing '40 Miles for 40 Acres' campaign — this time from Lawnside's historic Peter Mott House to the New Jersey State Capitol — spotlighting two reparations bills now before the Legislature.
posts.content:
Rev. Dr. Robert Turner, pastor of Empowerment Temple AME Church and a Commissioner with the National African American Reparations Commission (NAARC), has completed the 46th walk of his ongoing "40 Miles for 40 Acres" campaign — a 40-mile journey from the Peter Mott House, a documented Underground Railroad site in Lawnside, New Jersey, to the State Capitol in Trenton.

The walk, completed on July 14, 2026, drew attention to an active petition that calls on the New Jersey Legislature to pass two specific bills: A1665, establishing a New Jersey Reparations Task Force, and A5253, the Truth, Reconciliation, and Repair Act of New Jersey.

The event reflects Rev. Turner's sustained commitment to reparations advocacy — not as an abstract political conversation, but as a concrete legislative push with specific bills, specific deadlines, and a growing coalition of support.

**The Walk and Its Significance**

The choice of starting point — the Peter Mott House in Lawnside — was deliberate and symbolic. Lawnside is one of the few municipalities in the northern United States that was incorporated by African Americans before and after the Civil War. The Peter Mott House, a documented stop on the Underground Railroad, connects the current reparations conversation directly to the physical history of Black freedom and resistance in New Jersey.

The evening before the walk, Rev. Turner held a community conversation at the Burlington Quaker Meeting House — a site where Quakers have gathered for over 300 years, and one of the earliest religious communities in the United States to take a formal stand against slavery.

**Why New Jersey**

New Jersey holds a specific and often underexamined place in the history of American slavery. It was the last northern state to abolish slavery, and its legacy of racial inequality is measurable and documented. The petition Rev. Turner is championing cites several key disparities: a $662,500 racial wealth gap between white and Black and Latino families, a homeownership gap of 76.6% white versus 41.3% Black, and the nation's worst Black-white incarceration disparity, with Black residents incarcerated at 12.5 times the rate of white residents.

Reparations task force legislation has been introduced and failed in New Jersey five times — in 2005, 2019, 2022, 2024, and now as A1665. More than fifteen municipalities, including Newark, Orange, and Essex County, have already passed local resolutions in support.

"Acknowledgment without accountability is incomplete," said Rev. Turner. "The path to genuine repair runs through Trenton."

The petition will continue collecting signatures before being formally delivered to legislators. To learn more or add your name, contact Rev. Dr. Robert Turner at RobertTurner15@Hotmail.com or follow @Revdrrobertturner on Instagram.

posts.title: Newark's Lincoln Park Music Festival Returns for Another Summer of House, Hip-Hop, Gospel & More
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: The Lincoln Park Music Festival — Newark's largest free outdoor multi-genre music festival — returns to historic Lincoln Park this summer with two weeks of House, Hip-Hop, R&B, Gospel, and more.
posts.content:
Every summer, historic Lincoln Park in Newark becomes something bigger than a festival. It becomes a gathering place — for House heads and gospel lovers, for hip-hop fans and jazz devotees, for families and communities who come together around what they share: a love of music, a pride in Newark, and a connection to something that's been building here for over twenty years.

The Lincoln Park Music Festival (LPMF) is back for another year, and it remains one of the largest free outdoor music festivals of its kind in the entire region. With an average annual attendance that reaches well into the tens of thousands, LPMF has grown from its origins as a three-day event in 2005 into a two-weekend institution that draws visitors from across New Jersey and the Northeast.

The festival features an eclectic multi-genre lineup spanning House Music, Hip-Hop, R&B, Gospel, Jazz, and more — showcasing Grammy Award-winning acts alongside the most exciting emerging talent in New Jersey. Alongside the performances, the festival includes programming in technology, digital media, and music education, staying true to its roots as more than a concert — it's a cultural experience.

The festival is presented by the Lincoln Park Coast Cultural District (LPCCD) and organized by Newark Arts through the Festivals United Newark platform. LPCCD produces community events and arts programming year-round, but this annual festival is its signature moment — a celebration of Newark's identity as a city where music is woven into the fabric of everyday life.

Lincoln Park's House Music Day remains the festival's most anticipated single event — an electric, hours-long celebration of the genre that has always called Newark home. It's a day where the dance floor extends across a park, where generations find each other in the music, and where Newark's connection to the global House Music movement gets its proper recognition.

The festival is free and open to the public. Accessible via mass transit, with shuttle services typically available from various parts of the city to the Arts & Education District.

For the most current lineup, schedule, and ticketed event information, visit newarkarts.org or follow @lincolnparkmusicfestival on Instagram.

posts.title: Tampa's Creatology Residency Week Returns for Its 5th Year, Launching $4,000 Creative Roots Fund for Emerging Creatives
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Tampa's Creatology Residency Week is back for its 5th year — a six-day creative experience built on the belief that creatives don't let other creatives create alone. This year, the organization is launching a $4,000 Creative Roots Fund for deserving emerging artists.
posts.content:
Creatives don't let other creatives create alone.

That is the founding philosophy of Creatology, the Tampa-based organization that has spent five years building a space where artists, musicians, writers, poets, designers, and entrepreneurs can come together not just to network, but to connect, heal, and grow.

Creatology Residency Week returns for its 5th year, running Monday, July 6, through Saturday, July 11, 2026, in Tampa Bay. What began as a two-day creative conference has grown into a full six-day residency-style experience that draws creatives from across the country.

**The Creative Roots Fund**

This year's Creatology Residency Week is marking its milestone anniversary by launching the Creative Roots Fund — a $4,000 scholarship initiative designed to award two to three deserving emerging creatives with financial support for their artistic journey.

The fund reflects a core understanding that money is one of the most consistent barriers between creative people and their full potential. By removing that barrier — even partially — for a handful of emerging artists, Creatology is investing directly in the future of the creative community.

Fundraising for the Creative Roots Fund is ongoing leading up to the residency week. Those who want to contribute can do so through the Creatology organization's channels.

**About Creatology**

Creatology was founded by Janelle "J'Nelle" Richardson, who created the organization from a deeply personal place. Several years ago, Richardson was diagnosed with an anxiety disorder and began to understand how profoundly mental health affects creative output — and how isolated many creatives feel in their journey.

"I want creatives to remember that you do not have to do this all alone," Richardson said. "You are valuable, you are needed in this space, and you have a place where you can get your cup filled."

The six-day residency includes workshops, panels, networking events, and programming specifically designed for creatives working in music production, vocal performance, visual design, entrepreneurship, and storytelling. It is built for people who are serious about their craft and serious about building community around it.

**Why This Matters**

The creative industry has always had a mental health problem it rarely talked about publicly. The isolation of the creative process, the uncertainty of building a career in the arts, the financial instability that comes with creative work — these pressures are real, and they compound.

Creatology is one of the organizations addressing those pressures directly, not through platitudes but through programming, community, and now financial support for the creatives who need it most.

For information on attending or contributing to the Creative Roots Fund, follow @itscreatology on Instagram or visit the Creatology Eventbrite page.
